content: 1. Schneider S et al. investigated the presence of efavirenz in human breast milk, as well as in the plasma of mothers and their newborns. Their findings were published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2008 (Volume 48, Pages 450–454). 2. Gibb DM et al. examined pregnancy and infant outcomes among HIV-infected women undergoing long-term antiretroviral therapy (ART), with and without tenofovir, as part of the DART trial. The results were published in PLoS Medicine in 2012 (Volume 9, Article e1001217). 3. Benaboud S et al. measured the concentrations of tenofovir and emtricitabine in the breast milk of HIV-1-infected women in Abidjan, Côte d’Ivoire, as part of the ANRS 12109 TEMAA Study (Step 2). Their findings were published in Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy in 2011 (Volume 55, Page 1315). 4. Coutsoudis A et al. conducted a meta-analysis of individual patient data to assess late postnatal transmission of HIV-1 in breastfed children. The study was published in the Journal of Infectious Diseases in 2004 (Volume 189, Pages 2154–2166). 5. Kuhn L et al. evaluated the potential impact of the new WHO criteria for antiretroviral treatment in preventing mother-to-child HIV transmission. Their findings were published in AIDS in 2010 (Volume 24, Pages 1374–1377). 6. The WHO document titled Antiretroviral therapy for HIV infection in infants and children: towards universal access was accessed on May 15, 2013. 7. Newell ML et al. analyzed the mortality rates of both infected and uninfected infants born to HIV-infected mothers in Africa through a pooled analysis. The results were published in The Lancet in 2004 (Volume 364, Pages 1236–1243). 8. Dunn D et al. explored the relationship between current CD4 cell counts and the short-term risk of AIDS and death in HIV-infected children and adults before the availability of effective ART. The study was published in the Journal of Infectious Diseases in 2008 (Volume 197, Pages 398–404). 9. The Cross Continents Collaboration for Kids (3Cs4kids) Analysis and Writing Committee conducted a meta-analysis to identify markers predicting mortality in untreated HIV-infected children in resource-limited settings. The findings were published in AIDS in 2008 (Volume 22, Pages 97–105). 10. Raguenard M et al. reported excellent outcomes among HIV-positive children on ART in Cambodia, despite high pre-ART mortality and significant losses to follow-up. The study was published in BMC Pediatrics in 2009 (Volume 9, Article 54). 11. The National Guidelines on the Management of HIV in Rwanda (4th edition) were published by the Ministry of Health in Kigali in 2011. 12. Siegfried N et al. reviewed the optimal timing for initiating ART in HIV-positive, treatment-naive children aged 24 to 59 months. The findings were included in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (in press). 13. Puthanakit T et al. compared early versus deferred ART initiation in children older than one year infected with HIV in the PREDICT trial, a multicenter, randomized, open-label study. The results were published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases in 2012 (Volume 12, Pages 933–941). 14. Davies MA et al. used causal modeling to analyze when to start ART in children aged 2–5 years, presenting their findings at the 7th IAS Conference on HIV Pathogenesis, Treatment, and Prevention (June 30–July 3, 2013, Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia). 15. Penazzato M et al. assessed the programmatic impact of evolving WHO pediatric ART guidelines in resource-limited countries, with findings published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2012 (Volume 61, Pages 522–525). 16. Penazzato M et al. also explored healthcare worker perspectives on pediatric ART, contributing to the development of the WHO 2013 consolidated guidelines. These findings were presented at the 7th IAS Conference on HIV Pathogenesis, Treatment, and Prevention (June 30–July 3, 2013, Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia). 17. Barker PM and Mate K emphasized the need for significant improvements in maternal and child health services to eliminate mother-to-child HIV transmission. Their analysis was published in Health Affairs in 2012 (Volume 31, Pages 1489–1497). 18. Healy SA, Gupta S, and Melvin AJ reviewed HIV/HBV coinfection in children and the implications of antiviral therapy. Their findings were published in Expert Review of Anti-infective Therapy in 2013 (Volume 11, Pages 251–263). 19. Duncombe C et al. discussed the next phase of treatment, care, and support for HIV, as published in Current Opinion in HIV and AIDS in 2013 (Volume 8, Pages 4–11). 20. Shubber Z et al. conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of adverse events associated with nevirapineand efavirenz-based first-line ART. The study was published in AIDS in 2013 (Volume 27, Pages 1403–1412).
